source.title: Investigating Bias Representations in Llama 2 Chat via Activation Steering

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present. Some figures are represented by captions or flattened text.
record.tranche_reason: The study applies activation steering, including subtraction of a refusal vector, and reports response outcomes. It does not use the claim’s stated harmful-minus-harmless refusal-direction construction or test ablation at every layer and position.
record.gate_note: The paper reports only qualitative response outcomes for the steering experiments. It does not report a refusal-rate measure or general-capability evaluation. Its bias-vector transfer examples concern transfer between bias dimensions, not the transfer settings in V6.
record.test_reason: The study subtracts a refusal CAA vector, taken from Rimsky's red-teaming post [9], as a tool to elicit biased outputs from Llama 2 7B Chat. It reports only qualitative examples of whether bias appears, with no refusal rate. The refusal vector's construction is not described in the paper and is not shown to be a harmful-minus-harmless difference-in-means direction. There is no addition test for inducing refusal and no capability check. It also does not study whether jailbreaks naturally suppress the direction: the authors suppress it on purpose as their own red-teaming method. So no version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also report that Llama 2 7B Chat shows gender bias even without steering, and that bias is negatively related to refusal. They interpret the higher bias-vector similarity after RLHF as the model lumping biases together under topics it should refuse.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses contrastive stereotype-versus-anti-stereotype bias vectors and combines bias-vector addition with refusal-vector subtraction. It does not report the claim’s harmful-versus-harmless refusal-direction construction or its all-layer, all-position ablation.
record.method_sensitivity: The qualitative outcome depends on combining bias-vector addition with refusal-vector subtraction: bias addition alone led to refusal, and refusal-vector subtraction alone produced generic responses. The paper also notes that the racial bias vector was likely most effective because it used the largest sample size.

fits_no_version.finding: In Llama 2 7B Chat, gender, race and religion bias CAA vectors are negatively cosine-associated with the refusal CAA vector across layers 10–31. Gender is the least negative.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Bias steering vectors are anti-aligned with the refusal steering vector in Llama 2 7B Chat.

fits_no_version.finding: Subtracting a refusal vector while adding a bias vector elicits biased content that bias addition alone cannot. The model still verbally claims it cannot respond.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Refusal-vector subtraction is needed for activation-steering bias red-teams of RLHF chat models.

record.problems: The relevant steering outcomes are qualitative examples or descriptions, with no reported refusal-rate metric, uncertainty estimate, or general-capability check. The refusal-vector construction and exact subtraction settings are not stated in the paper text.
record.rows_left_out: No rows for the paper’s transfer examples between gender, race, and religion bias vectors, or its base-versus-chat comparisons of bias-vector similarities: these concern bias representations rather than the refusal-direction transfer or training claims in the versions listed.

untested.parts: The refusal vector's construction is unspecified (taken from [9]). There is no refusal-rate measure for ablation, no addition test inducing refusal, and no capability check.
There is no analysis of whether existing jailbreaks suppress the direction, and no training against ablation.
Not studied. Bias–refusal cosine similarity is not a harm-judgment-versus-refusal test.
The refusal vector is not compared between base and chat models. Only bias-vector similarities are compared.
The RLHF comparison concerns bias-vector similarity, not the refusal direction.

record.verdict_notes: The record's reader labels (V1 limits_scope, V3 supports/limits_scope) are dropped. The evidence is qualitative examples from the authors' own steering method, using an unspecified CAA refusal vector, and gives no refusal rate.

versions.untested_parts: Does not establish that the refusal vector was constructed as a harmful-minus-harmless difference-in-means direction; does not test adding the refusal vector to induce refusal, ablation at every layer and position, or preservation of general abilities.
No weight edit or released-model abliteration is tested.
Tests activation steering that subtracts a refusal vector in a bias-red-teaming setting; does not test training against ablation for robustness.
Does not test whether refusal is represented by an affine set, cone, or multiple refusal directions.
Does not separately measure harmfulness judgment and refusal decision.
Does not test transfer of the refusal direction across languages, model variants, or base and instruct models.
Does not test whether refusal-training choices determine whether a removable refusal direction exists.

rows.subject: Llama 2 7B Chat
rows.operation_detail: Subtracted the refusal steering vector while adding the corresponding bias steering vector (coefficient +2); activations were re-normalized to preserve residual-stream norm.

conditions.value: Bias evaluation prompts; specific set not stated
Corresponding bias vector; dimensions not individually quantified in the reported outcome

rows.measure: Qualitative response behavior: whether bias steering elicited biased content while refusal was suppressed.
rows.baseline: With the bias vector alone, the model refused to answer.
rows.value: The model still said it could not respond, but proceeded to produce more biased content; examples included racism-related language and religion-based positions.
rows.note: The result combines bias-vector addition with refusal-vector subtraction. The text does not report a refusal rate or quantify the amount of biased content.
rows.check: The measure is qualitative elicitation of biased content under combined bias addition and refusal subtraction, i.e. the study's own red-teaming method. No refusal rate is given. The model still 'claims that it cannot respond', so refusal removal cannot be read beyond one example. V3 does not apply because this is deliberate steering, not an attack shown to work through the direction.

rows.subject: Llama 2 7B Chat
rows.operation_detail: Added the corresponding bias steering vector with coefficient +2, without subtracting the refusal vector.

conditions.value: Bias evaluation prompts; specific set not stated

rows.measure: Qualitative response behavior: whether bias steering elicited biased content.
rows.value: The model refused to answer and characterized the prompt as offensive and discriminatory, including when the authors tried much higher coefficients.
rows.note: Comparison condition for the combined bias addition and refusal-vector subtraction.
rows.check: Bias-vector addition alone with no refusal-vector operation does not measure any refusal-direction intervention. The baseline is the unsteered model, which already refused race and religion prompts (Section 4.1). The state 'absent' refers to bias elicitation, not to any version.

rows.subject: Llama 2 7B Chat
rows.operation_detail: Subtracted the refusal steering vector without adding a bias vector.

conditions.value: Bias evaluation prompts; specific set not stated

rows.measure: Qualitative response behavior: whether refusal-vector subtraction alone elicited biased content.
rows.value: The model produced generic responses and was not made more biased by default.
rows.note: This tests the refusal-vector subtraction as a component of the red-teaming approach, but does not report a refusal rate.
rows.check: Refusal subtraction alone is described only as giving 'generic responses'. No refusal rate is reported, and the measure is bias, not refusal. This is a validation control for the bias method, so it cannot show whether refusal was removed.

rows.subject: Llama 2 7B Chat
rows.operation_detail: Measured cosine similarity between each bias steering vector and the refusal steering vector across mid-to-late layers.

conditions.value: Gender, race, and religion bias vectors compared with the refusal vector

rows.measure: Cosine similarity between bias steering vectors and the refusal steering vector.
rows.value: The text states that every bias vector is negatively associated with refusal; exact values are presented in Figure 11.
rows.note: The text describes the association, but numerical cosine values are only available in the figure.
rows.check: Cosine similarity between bias and refusal vectors is a related construct, not a version's effect. Numbers appear only in Figure 11. It is correctly kept under fits_no_version.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Combined bias-vector addition and refusal-vector subtraction
reader_labels.reason: The model emitted biased content but continued to state that it could not respond, so the reported outcome is not complete removal of refusal; see r1.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Combined bias-vector addition and refusal-vector subtraction
reader_labels.reason: This combined steering condition elicited biased content despite the model’s refusal language, as reported in r1.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Refusal-vector subtraction without bias-vector addition, and bias-vector addition without refusal-vector subtraction
reader_labels.reason: Subtraction alone produced generic rather than more biased responses, while bias addition alone led to refusal; see r2–r3.
